entities.name: Guru Nanak
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Gurū Nānak Dev (1469–1539) was the founder of Sikhism and the first of the ten Sikh Gurus, born at Rai Bhoi di Talwandi (modern Nankana Sahib, Pakistan) into a Hindu family. His life and teachings transformed the religious landscape of the Indian subcontinent and gave birth to one of the world's largest religions, with over 25 million adherents today.

At approximately age 30, Nanak experienced a profound spiritual awakening: he disappeared while bathing in the Bein river and returned three days later with the declaration: 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim' — a radical rejection of religious exclusivism that became the foundational principle of Sikh theology. He spent the next two decades on four great missionary journeys (udasis) spanning the Indian subcontinent, Persia, Arabia (including Mecca and Medina), and possibly Tibet, engaging in dialogue with Hindu sages, Muslim Sufi mystics, and Buddhist monks. He taught through sabads (hymns) composed in multiple languages and dialects, collected after his death in the Adi Granth (1604).

Guru Nanak's teaching rested on three pillars: Naam Japna (meditation on God's Name), Kirat Karni (earning an honest living), and Vand Chakna (sharing with others). He established the langar (communal kitchen) that serves all regardless of caste or religion — a revolutionary social institution that challenged the Hindu caste hierarchy. He rejected idol worship, caste discrimination, and empty ritual in favor of direct, personal devotion to one formless God. His theology anticipated aspects of what Western scholars would later call 'social justice religion' by five centuries.

{"summary":"Guru Nanak (1469–1539) was the founder of Sikhism, born in Nankana Sahib (modern Pakistan) into a Hindu Khatri family, who proclaimed a radically egalitarian spiritual message: that there is one God (Ik Onkar), that all human beings are equal before God regardless of caste, gender, or religion, and that devotion, honest work, and sharing with others (Naam Japna, Kirat Karni, Vand Chhakna) constitute the path to liberation. His teachings became the foundation of the world's fifth-largest religion, with 25–30 million adherents.

At age 30, Nanak underwent a transformative experience — emerging from the Vein River after three days, saying 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim' — which he spent the next 24 years making reality through four great Udasees (journeys) covering an estimated 28,000 km across India, the Middle East, Persia, and Mesopotamia, engaging in dialogue with Hindu saints, Muslim Sufis, Buddhist monks, and Jain ascetics.

His hymns, collected in the Adi Granth (later Guru Granth Sahib), combine devotional poetry with philosophical depth in the Punjabi language. The langar (free community kitchen), which he institutionalized at Kartarpur, became Sikhism's defining symbol of radical equality — people of all castes eating together seated on the floor, still practiced in every gurdwara worldwide.

Nanak's message of human equality and devotion to a formless God represented a profound challenge to both the caste system and religious orthodoxy — establishing a tradition that has produced some of
